group.passage: For the Paiwan people of southern Taiwan, glass beads are far more than pretty decorations. Text A is from an interview with a young Paiwan bead artist. Text B is a sign next to a glass bead necklace in a museum.

passage_parts.label: A
passage_parts.title: Meet a Bead Artist
passage_parts.text: The artist grew up in a Paiwan village in Pingtung. “My grandmother kept a few old beads in a small wooden box,” she says. “She told me that every bead had a name and a story.” After high school, she learned to make beads from older artists in her village. “I heat colored glass over a very hot flame until it is soft, and then I shape it slowly,” she explains. “The glass must stay close to the fire. If it cools too fast, it cracks.” One bead can take her about an hour, and no two beads are exactly the same. Her favorite is the peacock bead. “It stands for love,” she says. “Long ago, it was an important gift at weddings between noble families. When I finish one today, I hope it will bring its owner a happy life.”

passage_parts.label: B
passage_parts.title: Paiwan Glass Bead Necklace
passage_parts.text: Glass beads are one of the three treasures of the Paiwan people, along with clay pots and bronze knives. An old story says that the ancestors of the Paiwan made the first beads from the eyes of dragonflies, so the beads were seen as gifts from the gods. In the past, only noble families were allowed to own them. Noble families pass these beads down from parents to children, and beads were given as gifts when a couple married. Important beads have their own names and stories, such as the “sun’s tear” and the peacock bead, which is also called the bead of the clouded leopard. Different patterns carry different meanings, such as love or protection. Today, Paiwan artists still make glass beads, and visitors can even try making one themselves.

translation_zh.text:
【引言】對台灣南部的排灣族來說，琉璃珠遠不只是漂亮的裝飾品。Text A 摘自一篇訪問年輕排灣族琉璃珠工藝師的報導；Text B 是博物館裡一條琉璃珠項鍊旁的說明牌。
【A 認識一位琉璃珠工藝師】這位工藝師在屏東的一個排灣族部落長大。「我的祖母把幾顆老珠子收在一個小木盒裡，」她說，「她告訴我，每一顆珠子都有自己的名字和故事。」高中畢業後，她向部落裡年長的工藝師學做珠子。「我把彩色玻璃放在很熱的火焰上加熱到變軟，再慢慢塑形，」她解釋，「玻璃一定要靠近火，如果冷得太快，就會裂開。」做一顆珠子大約要花她一個小時，而且沒有兩顆珠子是完全一樣的。她最喜歡的是孔雀珠。「它代表愛情，」她說，「很久以前，它是貴族家族婚禮上的重要禮物。今天每當我做好一顆，我都希望它能為主人帶來幸福的人生。」
【B 排灣族琉璃珠項鍊】琉璃珠和陶壺、青銅刀並列為排灣族的三寶。一個古老的故事說，排灣族的祖先用蜻蜓的眼睛做出了最早的珠子，所以琉璃珠被視為神明的禮物。過去，只有貴族家庭可以擁有琉璃珠。貴族家庭把這些珠子由父母傳給子女，新人結婚時也會以珠子當禮物。重要的珠子有自己的名字和故事，例如「太陽的眼淚」，以及又叫「雲豹之珠」的孔雀珠。不同的圖案有不同的意義，例如愛情或保護。今天，排灣族藝術家仍在製作琉璃珠，遊客甚至可以親手試做一顆。
